This study develops a novel, time-varying Poisson auto-regressive with exogenous covariates (TV-PARX) model, dubbed as TV-PARX-G, which extends the TV-PARX model to accommodate nonlinear dynamics and structural breaks.  A breaking-point detection mechanism is incorporated into the TV-PARX model to identify the exact time points of structural breaks.  An empirical illustration using simulated data demonstrates the TV-PARX-G model's ability to accurately identify nonlinear dynamics and structural breaks.  Furthermore, the model's effectiveness is validated through two real-world case studies: one involving air quality data in China and the other involving COVID-19 transmission data in Italy.  Compared to existing strategies, the TV-PARX-G model delivers superior performance based on structural break identification results.  The TV-PARX-G model also outperforms other candidates in model selection as measured by the Bayesian information criterion and Akaike information criterion.  Releasing the underlying TV-PARX-G model's dynamics and structural break information enables the generation of rich Poisson count time series, allowing for various analytical purposes.

This study presents the development of a novel method for determining the vertical aerosol optical depth (ako) utilizing wide-field photometry data from a fully uncalibrated network of telescopes. By utilizing the relative calibration provided by moon observations, we established a reliable optical depth value for a clear conditions reference period. Subsequently, we calculated ako values from the difference between clear conditions and polluted periods, found to be effective against noise and biases. Our results show that a significant dust outbreak in Western Africa in 2020 was accurately mapped with ako values ranging from 0.5 to almost 1, consistent with independent measurements from CALIOP and AERONET. The effectiveness of this technique in detecting ako values during the same outbreak was also confirmed by multiple ground-based optical depth measurement sites. On average, our method yielded comparable ako values to those from CALIOP, with a slight underestimation of about 10-20% and demonstrated its ability to detect aerosol layering with a vertical resolution of at least 2 km. The technique's ability to identify aerosol layers was further validated by the detection of a aerosol-free conditions reference period at the start of the Southern Hemisphere winter.

This study used quantum mechanics to simulate the behavior of a simplified protein model, and we investigated the accuracy and efficiency of different numerical methods in a widely used computer program by implementing them as an external module. We evaluated four general purpose numerical methods, Ab Initio, Hartree-Fock, MP2, and DFT, as well as three hybrid setups on the alanine dipeptide model, and assessed their performance in various configurations. Results showed that DFT usually yields accurate energy values but sometimes fails to converge, while Ab Initio methods are more reliable but less precise. On the other hand, DFT produces the most accurate structures more often than other methods. To further analyze the methods' effectiveness, we applied them to a series of conformational changes in the alanine dipeptide, and evaluated their ability to predict optimal structures and calculate energy differences. Ultimately, we determined the DFT hybrid PBE0 setup with fudge factors to be the most efficient and reliable choice for quantum mechanical simulations of small protein models in the same program.

Human-generated image descriptions have excelled visually-impaired users with accessibility needs. However, creating such descriptions is time-consuming and labor-intensive, limiting the potential for new images on the web to be described. To address this challenge, I propose an innovative approach to automatically generating image descriptions. This method uses a combination of generative models, initial training on vast datasets like Conceptual Captions, and further fine-tuning on smaller datasets provided by describers. In addition, I outline an extended version of the Image Description Dataset, consisting of over 800 categories from Visual Genome. I also introduce a novel evaluation metric to assess description quality, focusing on the accuracy of detected objects. Our results demonstrate significant improvements in description quality and accuracy compared to existing methods. Our code is available at https://github.com/ruwix/image-description.

We provide a novel approach to solving optimization problems in quantum field theory by rephrasing them as an optimal control problem, then deriving an equation that the optimizer satisfies, and finally showing how this equation fits into a broader framework of Euler-Arnold equations, whose applications in differential geometry ensure the existence of optimizers.

The majority of hadronic processes, despite the large mass of heavy quarks, exhibit characteristics of free field theory development. This analytic approach, based on QCD's second highest order in alphaS and lowest order electroweak theory, has been employed to study heavy quark interactions and the resulting formation of charmed mesons. Using this framework, researchers have successfully recalulated earlier findings on quark gluon interaction patterns and have extended the calculations to include specific charm decay constants and properties of charmed mesons.

This research explores the optimization of wideband waveforming techniques for wireless networks deployed in semi-hardened environments, focused on the topics of combined and overall network throughputs. A non-linear integer programming model is developed to optimize fair-throughput and overall-throughput for OWWNs, and a relaxed linear model is also proposed to serve as an upper bound for optimization. To resolve practical constraints of the model, an iterative algorithm is presented, combining progressive reformulation, batched integer linear programming, and throughput optimization. Furthermore, the research investigates the optimization of overall and combined network throughputs for AWWNs, utilizing a non-linear integer programming model and a linear model respectively. An empirical evaluation across multiple scenarios demonstrates the algorithm's effectiveness in optimizing both combined and overall network throughputs for both OWWNs and AWWNs, and the linear model serves as an upper bound for both scenarios.

Determining parton distribution functions (PDFs) is an intricate task as they require matching evolution equations, specifically the DGLAP equations, to accurately describe the transition from low to high energy scales. Conventional fits for PDFs typically use a closed-form approximation called NLO enhanced leading logarithmic (EL) and fail to account for complicated scenarios involving multiple sources of evolution. To address this limitation, we've developed a new approach called the "combined" strategy, combining both EL and NL corrections, and have successfully implemented it within the xFitter working group framework. Utilizing this method, we've successfully fitted PDFs at NLO accuracy for multiple scenarios, including fits to individual data sets and combined datasets, as well as fitting PDFs and the strong coupling constant simultaneously. Furthermore, we've successfully fitted an initial PDF set, which we've called MMP, consisting of 30 fluxes, 15 nucleon PDFs, and the strong coupling constant at a scale of a few GeV, fitting the combined NLO PDF and QCD evolution equations simultaneously.

A linear analysis has been performed to understand the behavior of turbulent fluctuations in reacting flows within a linearized framework of an established turbulence model. To utilize this analysis, a closed-form expression is necessary for the reaction rate; therefore, an extended form of the $k-\epsilon$ model was employed. A total of five different combustion models were evaluated and compared, with the best performance demonstrated by a newly derived thin reaction layer model. This model showed significant improvement over the traditional premixed model and resulted in better simulation accuracy. The closed-form expression enabled the optimization of model parameters through CALI, which further enhanced the thin reaction layer model. This optimized model outperformed all other contenders and delivered superior forecasts in various turbulent mixing scenarios.

We introduce a novel analytical solution for a cosmological constant problem within the context of an extended gravitational theory, where mass creates curvature through a non-local, modified Poisson equation. This modification takes the form of a simple polynomial relation between kinetic and potential gravitational components, bypassing the need for analytical continuation. This new approach to non-local gravity builds upon earlier models, with the key advantage of producing physically meaningful results for observable quantities. A spherically symmetric mass distribution can be represented in a way that avoids singularities at the boundary, allowing for a more precise mass-radius relationship to emerge. This relationship differs significantly from the standard general relativity prediction for a de Sitter vacuum, demonstrating that the new relation leads to a more convincing description of cosmological constants.

A multidimensional analysis of $K^{\ast}(892)$0 and $f_{2}(1020)$ interaction in proton-proton collisions at the center mass energy of 13 TeV, is performed using a data sample of 1.7pb^-1 collected by the ALICE detector at the LHC. The measurement is based on an analysis of 0+-2 particles systems produced in events featuring at least one $K^{\ast}(892)$0 or $f_{2}(1020)$. The resulting differential cross-sections are evaluated in laboratory momentum variables for systems containing $K^{\ast}(892)$0$K^{\ast}(892)$0, $K^{\ast}(892)$0$f_{2}(1020)$, $f_{2}(1020)f_{2}(1020)$, $K^{\ast}(892)$0$K$0 and $f_{2}(1020)$0$. The measurement extends to invariant masses up to 6 GeV for $K^{\ast}(892)$0$K^{\ast}(892)$0 and 5 GeV for $f_{2}(1020)f_{2}(1020)$. The analysis finds evidence for the formation of a scalar glueball-like state in the $m_{0}$\Ket$^2$ versus $m_{0}$\Ket$^2$ + $p_{0}^{2}$ dimensionless variable

This study examines the relationship between neutron star low-mass X-ray binaries (LMXBs) and millisecond pulsars (MSPs) within the Galactic center, drawing in part from the 3rd Fermi and the second Arecibo Pilot Survey. A revised binary neutron star population estimate shows a significant enhancement compared to previous studies. Based on a conversion rate of 0.2 between LMXBs and MSPs and assuming a uniform birth rate of pulsars, we find that nearly 20% of all neutron stars born in the past 10 million years remain as MSPs within a few parsecs of their formation site. Additionally, we observe no clear evidence of a population of young and middle-aged pulsars similar to that seen in supernubber remnants. Moderately energetic pulsar kicks appear to suppress the presence of young pulsars in many remnants, whereas extremely energetic kicks might explain the absence of some old pulsar populations, particularly in the cases of the Puppis A and Pencil Nebule remnants.

A bipartite graph is universally recognizable based on its topological properties. This implies that a straightforward, vertical drawing will indicate a bipartite graph if we can identify the neighbourhood of each vertex and determine when two neighbours share an edge. If we split a shared edge in a graph, we can create a new vertex at its location. This results in a modified graph where a planar drawing exists if the original graph is a bipartite graph. Conversely, if the modified graph is planar, the original graph is bipartite.

Recent attacks like Flush+Reload have been impeded in their effectiveness by regular cache systems due to their inflexible time granularity. To overcome this limitation, we developed HyperDegrade, a novel technique that enhances the efficacy of Flush+Reload attacks to pinpoint exact cache events and adapt to varying workloads. HyperDegrade's "degrade phase" allows for precise time granularity by refining the attack surface through deliberate cache pollution, while the "boost phase" leverages newly created conditions to optimize the attack. Our findings show that HyperDegrade significantly improves the efficacy of Flush+Reload attacks in both ideal laboratory settings and realistic cloud computing environments, demonstrating a 2.5 times enhancement in time granularity and a 10 times reduction in required traces in our experiments. Furthermore, our results indicate that HyperDegrade is highly effective in exploiting both local and remote cache hits, demonstrating a 2 times improvement in success rates and enabling the development of novel attacks like the "Covert Channel Hunt."

A local modification applied to a knotted link in a polynomial-thick subset of the plane is referred to as a diagonal move when it involves moving a crossing that is adjacent to a double cross-over (a 'Y' shape) and changing it. We demonstrate that in a regulated environment, a delta-complex structure cannot contract to a trivial link through a sequence of Reidemeister moves that include diagonal moves, unless the structure becomes regulated first.

In multi-agent systems where tasks are distributed and unpredictable, agents make decisions about taking on tasks based on their capabilities and the information they have. This paper investigates how different distributions of task difficulties impact the choices agents make when completing tasks and how it affects their overall performance. It formulates two distinct scenarios: one where agents know the task difficulty distribution and another where it remains unknown. To resolve these scenarios, the paper develops two collaborative learning frameworks: one that uses the historical data of task completions and another that utilizes the feedback from agents. Furthermore, it designs two artificial environments and implements three real-world experiments to test these frameworks and demonstrate their effectiveness. One environment is created where tasks resemble video games and another where tasks are similar to assembly instructions. One experiment investigates how different distributions of task difficulties affect agents' decision-making strategies and another explores the impact of the number of agents on performance. The results show that both frameworks yield comparable outcomes when the distribution of task difficulties is known but differ when it remains unknown. One experiment examines the ability of agents to learn from feedback in an unknown distribution scenario and another investigates the ability of agents to adapt to new task distributions. One experiment compares the effectiveness of both frameworks in assembling instruction-like tasks and another explores how different distributions of task difficulties impact agents' decision-making strategies when completing video game-like tasks.

We provide a general approach for determining if a group G acts regularly on a metric space X, focusing on the case where a normal subgroup acts simply transitively. A key component of this method involves understanding Cartesian decomposition, achieved through identifying pairs of simultaneously action-compatible subgroups within G. A subgroup $\mu$ is considered suitable for our purposes if it serves as a member of such a pair, thereby allowing for efficient calculation of distances experienced under $\mu$'s action. A regular action is confirmed through applying either an existing theorem or the described method, relying on either identifying suitable subgroups directly or employing previous results. A detailed example is provided, utilizing the method to verify the regularity of a certain action associated with the symmetric group $S_n$, involving a previously unknown integer value of n.

In our discovery, we found that the binary neutron star system GW190521 showed anomalous behavior by deviating from the predicted relationship between gravitational wave slope and signal frequency. To better understand this phenomenon, we examined possible physical explanations, considering either a new theoretical model or an anomalous measurement. If the model is correct, a similar binary system with a delta omega value over 10 times larger should emit a gravitational wave within the sensitivity range of a future, more sensitive sloshing-Sagnac interferometer design.

This paper proposes a new random access protocol called NOVR-XL RA for XL-MIMO systems, addressing the challenges of massive feedback and statistical knowledge requirements. A non-adaptive, variable-length protocol is suggested, allowing for the optimization of medium access slate sizes through a machine learning approach called NOVR-XL RA. To further enhance the protocol's efficiency, a NOVR-XL RA-based slate construction algorithm is developed, utilizing an extended reinforcement learning interface called NOVR-XL RE. The proposed NOVR-XL RA protocol demonstrates significant improvements over existing protocols, showing a 20% boost in average slate size and a 50% reduction in average feedback bits in 16x16 XL-MIMO systems under moderate SNR levels.

Neural language models have significantly large contextual needs, making them impractical for use in many real-world language tasks. On the other hand, $N$-gram models are straightforward to use but lack the semantic understanding of neural models. We propose a novel framework that leverages the strengths of both models by using neural models to train neural $N$-gram models with a contextual extension, effectively meeting the contextual needs of neural models. Our method allows for the combination of neural models and enables the use of neural-based systems in tasks such as machine translation and summarization. Our findings demonstrate that our approach yields comparable or better performance compared to fully trained neural networks in many cases, and it also outperforms fully trained networks in several translation tasks as shown in our results.

This research seeks to address the persistent issues of optical character recognition (OCR) errors in vote tabulation systems, particularly in local elections, by developing a context-based spell correction algorithm. Our proposed algorithm, which we call ContextSpell, utilizes a combination of generative and contextual techniques to accurately correct OCR mistakes on ballot titles. To evaluate the effectiveness of ContextSpell, we created a large-scale dataset mirroring real election ballot titles, incorporating both perfect and imperfect OCR scans. Compared to established spell correction tools, ContextSpell demonstrates substantial improvements in OCR accuracy, according to both exact and contextual matching standards, respectively boosting overall accuracy by 37.5% and reducing errors by 60.6% on contextual matches.

This research used high-resolution models to mimic and study Mars' atmospheric behavior, particularly baroclinic storms, under conditions resembling those on the Martian polar ice caps during the planet's polar winter. Notably, we discovered similarities between these Martian storms and specific circulation patterns in a proposed Earth-like atmosphere, which featured a warm equatorial region and a mid-latitude jet stream. Through these comparisons, we identified analogous patterns between the Martian storms and the Earth-like atmosphere's circulation patterns, specifically the development of baroclinic disturbances and the formation of high and low-pressure areas. Additionally, we observed that the Martian storms' intensity and frequency were directly influenced by the polar ice caps' size and the release of heat from the ice, mirroring the impact of polar ice caps on a possible future Earth-like atmosphere, which would feature a warm polar region due to the polar ice caps' insulating effect.

We develop a novel method for constructing complex representations of special functions using Hankel paths in the complex plane. Building on the idea of scaling a Brownian motion, we create a complex stochastic process that represents a Hankel path and derive its associated Feyerman-Kac-type integral representation. As a key outcome, we obtain a complex representation of the Gamma function using this process. Moreover, we extend this representation to the complex gamma function's generalization, allowing non-integer values.

Quantum systems' initial non-equilibrium configurations frequently lead to complicated situations where steering phenomena occur. Although advanced methods such as linearized stochastic hydrodynamics can speed up the simulation of non-equilibrium conditions, it remains uncertain how these methods affect quantum correlations within the simulation. To address this, we developed and tested a linearized stochastic hydrodynamic scheme within the stochastic hydrodynamic theory, incorporating both harmonic oscillators and spin systems. The plan involves redefining non-equilibrium configurations through quantum correlations (both entanglement and steering) and investigating if the linearized stochastic hydrodynamic scheme accurately reproduces these changes. The research involves quantifying entanglement using the von Neumann entropy and investigating the anharmonic Mach-Zehnder interferometry. The results show that both linearized and full hydrodynamic schemes coincide in reestablishing equilibrium conditions. Additionally, the linearized stochastic hydrodynamic scheme effectively replicates both quantum correlations and vehicles used to manipulate light in an anharmonic Mach-Zehnder interferometry. The research also involves investigating a multi-partite system consisting of three harmonic oscillators, demonstrating that both linearized and full hydrodynamic schemes mirror non-equilibrium configurations through quantum correlations.

Our proposed method, called Knowledge-Aggregation-Regularized (KAR), extends the Teacher-Student architecture by adding a regularizing component between the teacher and student networks. During training, KAR minimizes the difference in output distributions between the teacher and student networks. Our method is not a new loss function but rather incorporates existing ones, allowing for the optimization of both the teacher and student networks jointly. We demonstrate KAR's effectiveness in various scenarios, including image classification and an adaptive bitstream compression application. Our results show that KAR consistently outperforms existing methods, achieving higher accuracy with significantly less parameter growth. For example, in the ImageNet classification test, KAR achieves a 10.2% accuracy boost over the state-of-the-art method.

We introduce Bucket Elimination with Sorting (BES), a variable-ordering graphical model inference and optimization method that builds upon Bucket Elimination (BE). Our BES algorithm combines the efficiency of BE with the tractability guarantees of variable ordering strategies like Min Fill (MF) and Sort First (SF). Our BES approach is particularly relevant for scenarios with large, complex models and sparse data sets, and we demonstrate its effectiveness through both theoretical proofs and practical demonstrations. Specifically, we prove that BES with the SF strategy only needs to reconsider previously optimized join trees in response to model updates, and we show that BES outperforms standard BE and becker's recursive BE (rBE) in both optimized and reoptimized scenarios. Moreover, we demonstrate that BES with the MF strategy (bms) can efficiently handle large, complex models by reusing existing join tree data, and we illustrate the algorithm's capability to handle massive models with extremely large fill-ins, as well as its ability to efficiently update join trees in response to model updates.

We provide explicit, closed-form expressions for the Hilbert-Poincaré series of centralizer $Z(\mathfrak{n})({\mathfrak s}{\mathfrak l}_2)$ and its graded version, as well as analogous series for $Z(\mathfrak{n})({\widehat {\mathfrak s}{\mathfrak l}_2})$ and $Z({\widehat {\mathfrak n}}({\widehat {\mathfrak s}{\mathfrak l}_2))$ by utilizing the integral formula and a combination of known series in the variable $q$.

We introduce an exact algorithm for the paired-permutation test that enables consistent statistical analysis even with nested permutations. This new algorithm proves to an analytical alternative to the normal distribution assumption for paired data and allows for large-scale, non-restricted inference. It is particularly effective for paired-permutation tests and paired big data sets. Our results show that this new exact algorithm offers similar performance to the normal distribution assumption for paired data and significantly outperforms the standard large-z test for nested permutations. It also provides higher statistical power by reducing the paired-permutation test area as much as the normal distribution assumption allows. A theoretical analysis showed that this new exact algorithm provides similar efficiency to the normal distribution assumption for paired data but reduces the paired-permutation test area. It is highly efficient and provides higher statistical power for paired-permutation tests and paired big data sets.

We establish a surprising connection between triangular and elliptic flow's transverse momentum dependence for specific particles. Initially, due to geometric preferences, we see a larger triangular flow ($\delta f_3$) compared to elliptic flow ($\delta f_2$) in inclusive particle distributions. However, once we isolate particles originating from the core region in Au+Au collisions, we find that $\delta f_3$ is actually smaller than $\delta f_2$. This shift in ratio indicates that triangular flow's transverse momentum dependence starts to diverge from elliptic flow's only after particles have undergone significant $p_T$ escalation, suggesting a link between flow patterns and particle transverse momentum distributions. Additionally, we observe that both $\delta f_3/\delta f_2$ and $v_3/v_2$ ratios exhibit similar transverse momentum dependence for different collision systems, implying that both ratios share a similar underlying similarity, likely rooted in collective, anisotropic fluid dynamics rather than initial state anisochronism.

This research develops an enhanced algorithm for identifying unverified target candidates, addressing the issues of sensor limitations and partial observations in dynamic networks. A novel approach has been created to estimate potential target movements, incorporating both sensor constraints and partial observations. This method enables the detection of previously unknown targets within a crowded space, using limited sensor fields of view. Compared to existing strategies, this method yields significantly improved results in terms of computational complexity, according to experimental results from the CARLoCO dataset and real-world sensor data from the PETS2013 dataset. The proposed algorithm outperformed existing methods in detecting new targets in the dynamic network context, on the CARLoCO dataset and a large-scale airport scenario.

We examine the decision to shoot or maintain possession of the ball in soccer, with a focus on situations resulting from opponents' mistakes or loss of control. Our research uses a large dataset of professional soccer matches to compare the expected reward of taking a shot versus regaining possession, with rewards assigned to shots, goals, and subsequent shots taken. We find that regaining control following a foul committed against the team or an errant pass generally leads to a higher expected reward than a shot, whereas a corner kick or throw-in typically yields a higher reward than a shot. However, we observe no significant difference in reward potential between taking a shot and regaining possession after a goal is scored, as well as no notable difference after the ball goes out due to a foul or an offside decision.

The integration of artificial intelligence (AI) into scientific research has been increasingly prominent, particularly within the physics community, as evidenced by the growing number of automated experimental setups. This trend is particularly notable in particle physics, where the shift towards distributed working arrangements, prompted by the pandemic, has created new opportunities for AI to streamline laboratory operations. In response to this development, researchers have begun exploring the potential of embedding AI decision-making capabilities within automated setups, allowing for more independent and self-managing experiments. This article presents a novel framework for using machine learning models on embedded devices to analyze data from particle physics experiments, marking a significant milestone in the automation of experimental setups. This achievement paves the way for the creation of fully autonomous experiments, capable of operating independently without human intervention, and highlights the potential for AI to revolutionize scientific research.

We investigate the stability of solitary waves in a system that incorporates a Klein-Gordon equation and an anharmonic oscillator, situated in a one-dimensional setting. By analyzing the appropriate evolution equation, we determine the conditions necessary for the stability of solitary wave solutions, as well as the behavior they exhibit as they evolve over time. We then proceed to identify specific solitary wave solutions that are unstable in the described anharmonic oscillator-Klein-Gordon system, but remain stable in variants of the system that include a Klein-Gordon equation, an anharmonic oscillator, and a massless Klein-Gordon equation, all arranged in a one-dimensional configuration. Our findings highlight the pivotal role that the anharmonic oscillator plays in stabilizing solitary wave solutions, as well as the importance of the interaction strength, oscillators' mass, and the wave's speed in determining the stability of these solutions.

The paper discusses the potential detection of long-lived neutral particles at colliders, focusing on the specific case of the decay product $R_d\to\mu\tau$. A novel search approach is proposed, differing from traditional methods that rely on decay lengths of a few meters, due in part to detection limitations for long distances. However, a particle physics model has recently been suggested, indicating the decay length could potentially reach 100 meters, necessitating a more effective detection strategy. A new search strategy is developed, utilizing the remaining energy of the particle after decay, which can leave significant destruction paths in jetting media such as quark glue systems before hitting the detector. This approach offers the possibility of detecting decay lengths up to 100 meters, and demonstrates its feasibility using simulated data from the ATLAS detector, showing detection potential for the proposed particle physics model.

A substantial challenge in understanding language models lies in their inconsistent behavior when processing context with varying levels of specificity. While models excel at identifying precise terms in context, they often struggle when confronted with more general terms, even when the underlying relationship remains the same. To better grasp this phenomenon, our study introduces the concept of "relation contextualization", examining how language models perceive relationships between terms in context. We propose an experimental design where models must recognize established connections between unrelated words, differentiating between general and specific forms of these words. To create these conditions, we utilize controlled contexts with adjustable levels of specificity. Our results indicate that pre-trained language models frequently misinterpret highly specific contexts in favor of highly general contexts, despite the availability of more suitable options. To address this issue, we outline the theoretical foundation for a relation contextualization task and design a novel dataset comprising 1,600 relation contextualization experiments. After fine-tuning language models on this dataset, we observe significant improvements in recognizing relationship-based context, coupled with enhanced performance in downstream tasks. Our findings suggest that language models can be trained to accurately identify relationships between words in context, even when models struggle initially, and advocate for the utilization of relation contextualization in research and applications.

A recent paper has been inconsistent with a widely accepted model of dark matter behavior by suggesting that certain heavy nuclear states decay too quickly when interacting with dark matter. To address these findings, we must first consider a different perspective on the dark matter model. It is proposed that ultra-low mass particles might actually interact stronger with dark matter, which could explain their lack of observation. However, this new idea also creates complications as it conflicts with established theoretical predictions of how dark matter behaves when interacting with ultra-low mass particles. To resolve this issue, it is proposed that the standard model's electroweak sector needs to be extended to higher energies. In doing so, we can readjust the theoretical predictions to accommodate the new idea of stronger dark matter interaction with ultra-low mass particles. Ultimately, the revised framework suggests that the smallest possible particle mass, as predicted by certain theoretical models, might actually interact weaker with dark matter than others of similar characteristics.

A new class of quantum systems has been discovered, where continuous driving forces a quantum harmonic oscillator into a state of coherent motion. Despite the fact that coherent states are unstable in isolated quantum oscillators, they have been found in systems driven by continuous light and subjected to an environment that rescues the oscillator. A novel theoretical framework has been developed to describe such stabilized coherent states within the context of an driven quantum harmonic oscillator in an environment. A general approach was derived to calculate the characteristics of coherent states, including their stability, as well as the minimal driving intensity required to achieve that state. Moreover, the theoretical findings have been validated through numerical simulations.

We develop a quantum relational Hoare logic that enables the verification of programs' output sensitivity to specific input components. This logic extends the existing quantum relational Hoare logic to positively confirm the appearance of character traits and to negatively confirm the absence of distracting components. We demonstrate how to prove that a program meets certain output specifications by applying this new logic and then compile the verified specifications into quantum programs. Our method allows for the precise quantification of output sensitivity in a simple quantum program that sorts two character strings.

This research explores utilizing chromatic data to accurately determine magnetic fields on the solar surface, particularly in areas with significant magnetic activity. Vector magnetic field maps are commonly derived from spectro-polarimetric observations using inversion algorithms like the Minimum Marrelli-Rubiño (MUR) code, which assumes a fixed magnetic fill fraction. However, this assumption can lead to inaccuracies when maps are obtained from data with varying chromatic properties, such as SDO/AIA and GONG. To address this issue, we propose using SDO/HMI Intensity Grams to determine the magnetic fill fraction before inverting the spectro-polarimetric data. Our method involves using a simple threshold to calculate the fill fraction for simple structures, and utilizing a more complex model like BACULA for more intricate cases. To apply this model, we need to fit a structure template, which can be a simple loop or a more complex shape like an $\Omega$-loop. To evaluate the effectiveness of this approach, we conducted a comparison with the standard method using a fixed fill fraction for a simple structure, and analyzed three different events observed between 2017 and 2020. The results showed that the fill fraction often exceeds 50%, which is the limit for the MUR code, indicating that it is not always applicable. Nevertheless, by adjusting the fill fraction, we can obtain more accurate vector magnetic field maps that align with true values derived from local helioseismology. Furthermore, this method can be

We provide explicit, countable sets that generate Coxeter groups of rank two within certain specified interval boundaries, deviating from previous descriptions. Specifically, we demonstrate that for a Coxeter system (W, S) where the group depth is infinite and the generating set size is greater than 3, the number of spheres in the wedge complex at the center of the cube labeled by S' remains countable.

This research paper introduces the concept of invariant shapes for higher-order tangential derivatives in the context of the Euclidean sphere and the hyperbolic plane. It is demonstrated that certain geometric shapes, specifically Bertrand curves, do not have uniquely defined second normal derivatives in specific geometric spaces, unless certain conditions are met. The paper also delivers original results on a distinctive type of curve called the "simple and regular Apollonius curve," which represents a curve shaped in a way that both first and second normal derivatives are uniquely defined. A step-by-step approach is used to calculate the formula for an Apollonian curve in the Euclidean sphere, and an outline of how to reconstruct a curve from its first and second normal derivatives in the hyperbolic plane.

This research explores the creation of diverse loss functions for a single image and develops various loss representations. Unlike traditional methods that focus on a small number of loss functions, our approach utilizes multiple loss functions to enhance a state-of-the-art few-shot learning model. Our underrepresented loss function dataset, which includes 900 loss function instances, was generated using the developed framework. After optimizing the most representative 50 loss functions, our method achieves the best few-shot learning performance, according to current standards. On 5-way 1-shot N-way class classification tasks on FC100, our method delivers significant improvements of 1.8% compared to TADP, and 1.0% compared to TAML, while reducing the search time by 22.5 times.

Neural models have excelled at identifying if-then relations in text, achieving impressive performance with relatively little labeled data. In recognition of the simplicity and effectiveness of these models, researchers are working to better understand the factors that contribute to the success of these models. This paper extends our previous study on categorizing if-then relations into distinct types, which we have dubbed the Basic Relation Type Hierarchy. Our findings show that neural models perform well at recognizing relations in line with this hierarchy, demonstrating that only a small amount of labeled data is required to train these models for each relation type. Furthermore, we observed that the performance of these models improves significantly when they are trained on relations categorized within this hierarchy, prior to being tested on new, unseen relations. One notable discovery was that neural models can recognize relationships between categories, allowing them to learn from relations they have not been explicitly trained on. Our research also led to the creation of a new dataset consisting of annotated texts with if-then relations, which is currently lacking in the field.

We introduce the novel viewpoint video prediction problem as a research challenge and develop a dynamic neural graphics model called ViewTransform.  A key component of ViewTransform is a novel dual representation called dual feature embedding, which enables seamless manipulation of camera angles.  Our primary contribution lies in a dynamic texture network called DynamicTextureN, which generates detailed video content.  Our method ViewTransform outperforms the state-of-the-art models by achieving significant gains of 6.34 and 8.83 in SSIM scores on the Chair and Car datasets respectively.  Our dynamic texture network DynamicTextureN delivers superior performance over the ground truth in various datasets by achieving gains of 3.24 and 2.53 in SSIM scores on the Chair and Car datasets respectively.

We introduce the concept of a partially evaluated graph, where only information about geodesic paths between specific pairs of vertices is known. Building on this idea, we define a sub-dimension $\delta_\kappa(\G)$ of a graph's metric dimension when we set a threshold $\kappa$ for the geodesic distance between vertices. We demonstrate that determining the number of vertices in a partially evaluated graph that has a specified sub-dimension $\delta_\kappa(\G)$ is essentially hard. However, by applying the algorithm for minimum-weight matching, we can solve the problem efficiently. We observe that in treewidth-$t$ graphs, we can determine the number of vertices in a sub-dimension $\delta_\kappa(\G)$ within polynomial time when the threshold $\kappa$ is limited and the graph's structure is known. We also investigate the idea of "skipping" distances in vertex orderings, demonstrating that in planar graphs, we can determine the number of vertices in a sub-dimension $\delta_\kappa(\G)$ within polynomial time when the threshold $\kappa$ is limited.

This research develops an enhanced automatic system for identifying heart health issues using acoustic cardiogram recordings, as part of our broader project to tackle the Task 1A challenge at the Intent Intent Understanding Workshop. Our initial prototype, described in our previous paper, yielded impressive results; however, we noticed its sensitivity to noise and motion artifacts. To address these limitations, we have designed and implemented three novel noise-reduction algorithms: an adaptive Wiener hybrid method, a learning-based signal processing model, and a shallow neural network that learns feature representations suitable for cardiac health analysis. We have tested these algorithms on the challenge's development set and incorporated them into our existing framework, leading to notable improvements in accuracy. The most effective algorithm, the adaptive Wiener hybrid method, demonstrated a 27% boost in accuracy and achieved a remarkable overall accuracy of 99.4% on the development set. We have also created two additional tasks to enhance the system's capabilities: classifying cardiac health issues using electrocardiogram recordings and analyzing exercise-induced changes in acoustic cardiogram data.

We present a multi-wavelength observational study of the massive starburst galaxy, Mrk 477, utilizing a vast range of data, including X-rays from Chandra, optical rotation curves from the Integral Field Unit (IFU) of the SINFONI instrument, optical spectroscopy from Keck, and far-ultraviolet spectroscopy from the Hubble Space Telescope. The large extent of the circumgalactic medium (CGM) and the low central velocity dispersion in Mrk 477 enable us to investigate the connection between star formation, gas reservoirs, and the wind behavior for the first time in an extreme starburst galaxy. The high stellar mass growth rate in Mrk 477 leads to significant supernova feedback, resulting in strong low-density molecular winds detected through the absence of metal I lines and the presence of CI lines. The comparison of CI lambda 6371 and CI lambda 926 (or CI lambda 9851 in the case of low signal-to-noise data) line ratios in different galactic regions allows us to identify areas with either molecular winds or CGM reservoirs. The line ratios of CI lambda 6371 to CI lambda 9851 correlate inversely with the velocity dispersion of the gas, while the CI lambda 926 to CI lambda 6371 ratio remains constant. We establish explicit formulae for the velocity distribution of a second-class particle in ASEP (Asymmetric Simple Exclusion Process) and TASEP (Treiber-Avjeshich-Elandser Process), which are both linear irreversible Markov chains on an integer lattice. The derived formulae involve products of harmonic analytic functions on complex vector spaces, enabling the calculation of expected velocities for any initial condition of particles. Furthermore, we prove that the TASEP and ASEP processes converge to the same limiting distribution as the lattice size increases, demonstrating that they behave identically in the half-space problem. Additionally, we provide an alternative proof that the ASEP process satisfies the central limit theorem.

This study examines the characteristics of infectious diseases with a short incubation period, focusing on the biological limitations of such diseases. A novel method is developed for distinguishing between risk factors that contribute to infection and factors that contribute to disease manifestation, using differential privacy models and an approach called "structured Bayesian inference." This method is then applied to real-world data from the Contact Tracing Mobility Study in Germany, demonstrating its effectiveness in doing so. One advantage of this method is that it allows for the drawing of meaningful biological conclusions when structured.

This research examines the NUV-r color of galaxies at varying masses, using data from the Sloan Digital Sky Survey (SDSS) and GALEX. Contrary to expectations, we observe a positive trend in NUV-r color in relation to galaxy mass, after adjusting for factors like stellar mass ratio and environment. Notably, this trend reverses when considering only massive galaxies. To understand this phenomenon, we developed an analytical model accounting for cold flows and gas accretion onto galaxies. Cold flows are postulated to lead to increased star formation, resulting in a tighter relationship between gas mass and stellar mass, and ultimately a more positive NUV-r color trend, before cold flows become negligible. Observing the microwave background as cold flow proxy, we calculate the mass density threshold for a given galaxy's environment. Based on the SDSS survey, we find a higher threshold density at higher galaxy masses, consistent with our model. Additionally, we observed a positive correlation between NUV-r color and redshift in similar galaxy environments, on a galaxy-by-galaxy basis, in the SDSS and z~1 data from the COSMOS field.

Multilingual language models have been successful in performing tasks such as translation and sentiment analysis. However, since these models are massive and require substantial computational power, researchers have explored the use of existing models trained on larger languages and train their smaller counterparts on the task at hand. This approach can be effective but often demands large amounts of trained data. In the case of sentiment classification in under-resourced languages, this approach has shown promise but is hampered by the need for labeled data. To address this challenge, our methodology utilizes a pre-trained multilingual model and adapts it for classification purposes in an under-resourced language by using unlabeled data from that language. Moreover, to enhance the workflow and eliminate the necessity of translated data, we employ the same pre-trained model for language translation. Specifically, we train our model using a mixture of naturally occurring translated data (from English to a given language) and naturally occurring sentimentally expressed data (in the given language). Our method has several advantages over existing approaches. For instance, it bypasses the requirement for translated training data, reduces the reliance on highly polished translated data, and eliminates the need for multiple models. Our findings, as demonstrated through extensive experiments on five under-resourced languages (Telugu, Marathi, Gujarati, Bengali, and Punjabi) and the use of the mT5 model, confirm the effectiveness of our methodology.

We report on the detection of unusual, chevron-shaped rotation profiles for KIC 9267654 in its magnetic and non-magnetic states. This star's rapid rotation and moderate mass make it an ideal candidate for studying differential rotation. However, unlike similar beta Hydri stars, KIC 9267654 doesn't exhibit a correlation between its rotation rates and profiles. To better understand this pattern, we examined the star's spectral types within different regions and their corresponding profiles. Noting that the beta and gamma regions exhibit similar rotation rates but distinct shapes, we propose that the Chevron-shaped profile is not solely the result of differential rotation. Instead, it may be influenced by the presence of a strong, asymmetric magnetic field or a combination of fields, which could also explain the observed variability in the profiles. Additionally, we observed a possible periodicity in the star spots for the beta and gamma regions, which could be linked to the stellar core convection. If confirmed, this would make KIC 9267654 one of the few stars exhibiting this characteristic, alongside HD 125353. Further research is necessary to verify this periodicity and explore possible causes, including the possibility of a rapid core rotation or the presence of a companion star inducing tidal forces.

Fake news has become a pressing concern on social media, and automated systems like ours aim to help curb its spread by effectively identifying false information. Our research introduces MetaFEND, a deep learning model that surpasses existing methods in detecting false information on Twitter. The MetaFEND model's superiority is demonstrated through comprehensive evaluations on three diverse datasets: BotOrNot, FakeNewsNet, and STNC. The results show that the three-task model consisting of a primary MetaFEND model and two identical smaller models at its tiers outperforms significantly when compared to a single large MetaFEND model. This optimized three-tier MetaFEND structure yields the best detection accuracy of 97.5% on the BotOrNot dataset, whereas individual large models are limited to 77.1% accuracy. Furthermore, the three-tier MetaFEND model leads to substantial reductions in computational costs without compromising detection accuracy.

A Golay complementary array pair is defined as two complementary partial Steiner systems, and we present necessary conditions for its quaternary incarnation to be feasible. This necessary condition can be expressed in a recursive form, allowing for its direct verification in simple cases. We also outline the initial values of an explicitly recursive sequence, which serves as a proof that our condition is indeed sufficient for binary Golay complementary array pairs to be feasible. However, integer recursion is not suitable for computational purposes, and instead, we provide an alternative, acute-angle recursive formula that is more practical for verifying the condition.

A recent surge in interest for COVID-19 research has led to the development of various algorithms for identifying lung infections in X-ray images. This work presents an innovative, shallow CNN-based approach that efficiently segments infected areas in COVID-19 images, thereby enabling the creation of valuable feature maps. A subsequent deep CNN is then applied to these pre-processed images to achieve high segmentation accuracy. This layered approach enables the construction of an all-purpose network that can be used to segment various medical image datasets including COVID-19, normal lung and tomographic images. This all-purpose network can be used to extract general feature maps which serve as valuable inputs to deep CNNs for segmenting diverse medical image datasets.

This study develops an integrated framework for both supervised and unsupervised feature extraction, targeting various machine learning models. The proposed framework, dubbed Adversarial Regularized Deep Hash, incorporates a layer that learns features through a shallow neural network and a layer that learns deep feature learning via a convolutional neural network. The framework's first component uses unsupervised regularized linear regression to learn hash functions, while the second component uses an adversarial regularized strategy to learn deep feature learning. We present a comprehensive set of algorithms as the framework's source code, title DeepHashNet.

Recent breakthroughs in question-answering tasks have been achieved by models trained on factual triples extracted from knowledge graphs, but this requires the creation of these triples, which is a time-consuming process.  Alternatively, models trained on large amounts of text data have been successful in question-answering tasks, but they struggle with triples-based evaluation.  In our research, we demonstrate that models trained on traditional text data can effectively answer question-answering tasks when evaluated using triples-based evaluation, as it learns general question-answering patterns in the process.  Our results show that models trained on text data perform at least as well as models trained on knowledge graphs in question-answering tasks, and in some cases, significantly better, as evidenced by our experiments on 16 question-answering datasets, consisting of 50 categories, across three large language models.  Our findings suggest that knowledge graphs are not inherently superior to large amounts of text data for training question-answering models, as it is possible to generate new triples-based evaluation data through the same process of creating general question-answering patterns, which is also supported by the performance of models trained on web crawled data in our additional experiments.  Our research offers a new perspective on the effectiveness of models trained on traditional text data in question-answering tasks, as it eliminates the need for extracting factual triples, which is a time-consuming process.

We conduct an investigation into the non-linear aspects of Yang-Mills charges within a framework of an external electric field, and explore how it impacts the structure and properties of charged AdS black holes. Building upon the Chern-Simons equation and a specific anisogamic gauge group, we define the non-linear Yang-Mills charge parameter through a radial dependent function. Counterintuitive mass loss is observed when increasing the non-linear Yang-Mills charge in certain scenarios. Additionally, we find that both the shadow radius and the near-horizon thermal profile of the black hole exhibit enhanced levels of non-linearity in response to increased charges. Furthermore, a direct, non-linear relationship is discovered between the Yang-Mills charge and the shadow radius. We also derive an integral equation that allows for the calculation of the scalar field profile around the black hole.

We undertook an in-depth analysis of how non-classical effects, specifically entanglement and spin-swap oscillations, appear in optical tomograms for a two-component harmonic oscillator model in a state of squeezed vacuum. To better understand these phenomena, we first derived exact expressions for the optical tomogram, as well as the von Neumann entropy in the same scenario. Subsequent quantum measurements, in the form of homodyne and balanced homodyne detection, were performed to investigate these non-classical characteristics. Our research findings showed that entanglement and spin-swap oscillations are directly reflected in distinct patterns in optical tomograms. Moreover, we observed that both the von Neumann entropy and the von Neumann entropy's peak location at the measurement point can be used effectively to predict the presence of entanglement and spin-swap oscillations. Finally, we explored various parameter combinations to further illustrate the correlation between these non-classical effects and the mentioned quantities.

Determining branching fractions for specific decay modes is a complex task, often influenced by limited data and simultaneous fit procedures. To address this challenge, I propose an integrated framework that leverages machine learning models to accurately predict branching fractions. Initially, I employ unsupervised learning to group decay modes into distinct categories based on their characteristics. Subsequently, supervised learning is used to develop models for each category, reducing the need for extensive decay data. To further enhance branching fraction determinations, I introduce a technique called systematic shift estimation, which accounts for potential uncertainties resulting from detector performance and theoretical inputs. To apply this framework, I have compiled a comprehensive dataset consisting of 240 known branching fractions, split equally between training and validation sets. To evaluate the framework's efficacy, I conduct sensitivity analyses to assess its resilience to various sources of uncertainty. Ultimately, I demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed method by achieving accurate branching fraction determinations for a sample of 80 known values.

We prove that for a module $M$ over a semisimple algebra $A$, having a simple component description with modules $S_1, \ldots, S_k$ and a submodule lattice lattice $\Gamma$ being reconstructible in polynomial time, the submodule lattice of $M$ can be accurately reconstructed in polynomial time. Moreover, the submodules of its composition factors $T_1, \ldots, T_l$ that arise from the product decomposition of $M$ have lattice structures $\Delta_1, \ldots, \Delta_l$ with which we can reassemble the lattice $\Gamma$ quickly.
We provide novel proofs that conformal and shape operators have recurrent Ricci tensors when biharmonic hypersurfaces are embedded in a Euclidean space and satisfy the minimal condition.

We provide a new definition for subsets of the set (Np/q)d that are recognizable by p/q-Det S-Automata. We then demonstrate that this definition is equivalent to the previously established definition through a finite-state automaton that identifies and avoids rational subsets.

This research focuses on three distinct approaches to describing decay rates in beauty quark decays: the CLN method, the BGL framework, and an alternative BGL-based approach. The data-driven BGL method with linear polynomial corrections was initially employed in our previous analysis. To utilize the BGL method with non-linear polynomial descriptions, new decay rate parameters are required. We derive these parameters using two different schemes: the BGL(2,2) and BGL(3,3) models. We then update our previous beauty decay width calculations using the BGL(2,2) and BGL(3,3) models, and re-analyze relevant decay data. The 3D unweighted average of $\Delta\Gamma_s$ remains unchanged at $0.0211 \pm 0.0024$. However, we observe that the BGL(2,2) and BGL(3,3) models yield similar results, indicating that the description of decay rates is not significantly enhanced by using non-linear polynomials. We also examine the relationship between the BGL and CLN methods, finding that the CLN $y_s$ parameter is directly related to the BGL $a_2$ coefficient, and concluding that further data is necessary to distinguish between these approaches.

This study examines the Lyapunov exponent's integral form and develops two novel numerical methods to compute it: the harmonic function (HF) approach and the iterative weighted derivative (IWD) method. The HF method is extremely efficient with a low computational cost, making it suitable for rapid determination of the exponent's stability properties. In contrast, the IWD method provides highly accurate results but comes at a higher numerical cost. To validate these methods, various applications were demonstrated across a range of complex dynamical systems, including the Lorenz system, the Kuramoto-Sivashinsky equation, the complex Ginzburg-Landau equation, and a simple hyperchaotic system. The results from both methods show excellent agreement and accurately reflect the system's dynamical characteristics. The findings demonstrate the methods' ability to effectively identify the source of exponent instability and can be used to confirm the existence of strange attractors in dynamical systems.

This study generalizes the concept of an angle function in a planar manifold to a broader class of spaces known as quasihyperbolic manifolds and expands on a result showing the embeddability of a domain in such a space through its use of a function satisfying an appropriate condition.  A quasihyperbolic manifold is defined as a space that is locally equivalent to a subset of an n-dimensional Euclidean space, modified to accommodate certain acute angles, and differs from a hyperbolic manifold only by the description of acute angles.  The study also delves into the topic of mapping quasihyperbolic manifolds onto higher-dimensional Euclidean spaces through the use of a function satisfying a specific condition.  A quasihyperbolic manifold is classified as a space that, at a local level, is similar to a subset of an n-dimensional Euclidean space, with certain acute angles accounted for, and the research finds that such a space is conformally embeddable if its underlying domain meets specific width requirements.  The study further explores the application of a quasihyperbolic manifold's shape to mapping areas in higher-dimensional Euclidean spaces through the use of a specific condition-requiring function, as well as expanding the domain of a quasihyperbolic manifold that is already defined as conformable through the use of a function satisfying a specific condition.  The study also examines the process of mapping quasihyperbolic manifolds onto higher-dimensional Euclidean spaces through the use of a specific

Our TPC model, achieved through the incorporation of invariant principles and learning techniques, demonstrates exceptional performance in varying twisting sensitivity levels on various point cloud models.  Compared to the conventional approach of using invariant principles alone, the TPC model exhibits enhanced certified accuracy in nearly all tested models across diverse twisting sensitivity levels.  At the highest sensitivity level of 32, the TPC model shows a significant improvement of three orders of magnitude in certified accuracy compared to the conventional method, achieving an average certified radius of 1.5 in models with large point clouds, and demonstrating excellent stability against complex twisting scenarios.  Moreover, our results indicate that the TPC model can recover the loss of certified accuracy resulting from the employment of multiple twisting sensitivity levels, showing no decline in certified accuracy when shifting from one twisting sensitivity level to another.  Our method enables the validation of symmetries in large point cloud models, allowing for the generation of realistic, physically consistent, ideally infinitely large model datasets of size three, and demonstrating superior certified accuracy compared to existing methods on all tested models.

A common challenge faced by programmers when working on parallel programs is identifying and fixing errors. To address this issue, we have developed an automated testing environment called ParalDux that offers real-time code suggestions and a repair tool that generates corrected code. By integrating ParalDUX into an integrated development editor, programmers can quickly locate and fix synchronization errors in parallel programs. An evaluation involving 15 developers on three different projects showed that the average time to find and fix an error was 2.5 minutes, with a success rate of 70.8% for real-world errors and 83.3% for artificially introduced errors. Compared to existing automated repair tools, ParalDUX outperformed them in six out of seven tested scenarios.

We establish an equivalence between G_K-Artin-Scheier cocycles and a specific subclass of reduced crystalline extensions through a direct construction. This construction involves a specific subset of Dieudonn'e modules resulting from reduced crystalline extensions and demonstrates that these cocycles precisely match the (gamma)-reduced, (gamma)-decomposable, and non-degenerate conditions. Moreover, we show that the reduction modulo p of a crystalline extension corresponds to the same cocycle it is isomorphic to, and that all relevant conditions are preserved under extension and restriction.

A piezoelectric polymer-based self-sensing composite material, similar to laminated composites, suffers from accurate damage identification limitations due to the non-linear relationship between electrical and mechanical signals. To address this challenge, a self-adaptive genetic algorithm was integrated with a neural network to enhance the capability of detecting damage in such materials. The primary contribution involves training the neural network using a genetic algorithm to match the initial carbon fiber tensile strain and electrical signal changes resulting from an unknown impact. Subsequent improvements were achieved by implementing multiple training sessions in series and using a self-adaptive genetic algorithm within each session. The results showed that the composite material's self-sensing capacity could be significantly enhanced when using a combination of neural networks and a genetic algorithm, or a single deep neural network, when compared to standard identification methods. Furthermore, technical feasibility was demonstrated by applying the optimized neural network framework to various impact scenarios and previously unknown loads.
We establish several integral identities involving the Bernoulli polynomials $B_n(x)$ and the Euler polynomials $\epsilon_n(x)$ by utilizing geometric vector proofs.

For a certain class of groups that extend free groups within their structure, specifically right-angled Artin groups and their actions on trees, we have found a key property. A defining feature of such an action, we've discovered, is either closed orbit or free action on the tree it acts upon. What's notable about this characteristic is it only pertains to actions within a specific subset of the group's actions, initiated by the actions of subgroups on the tree's structure, taking place within a sub-tree shaped by a distinct sub-graph of the group's structure.

This study examines how the Nested Neumann algorithm's convergence rate can be optimized for low-rank matrix completion by reintroducing the inception depth concept. Our modified inception depth hierarchy, consisting of average and subtracted layers, enables the creation of efficient convergence acceleration schemes. We derived a step-by-step implementation of the Nested Neumann algorithm using the revised inception depth hierarchy, which we then used to develop an alternating minimization algorithm for bilinear PCA. Our optimized scheme featuring five average layers and three subtracted layers outperformed previous optimized schemes. Our optimized scheme achieved the fastest convergence rate for bilinear PCA, allowing for the development of a more efficient low-rank matrix completion algorithm. Our findings demonstrate the algorithm's potential for wide applicability.
